item.title: PEOPLE | The one and only
item.description: Every Hibiscus season, memories come flooding back for Liebling Elizabeth Marlow — the young woman who, 70 years ago, made history as the inaugural winner of the Hibiscus Festival. As Fiji experiences another Hibiscus celebration this year, Liebling remains the only woman to hold the distinction of being the country’s first Hibiscus queen.
item.content:encoded:
Every Hibiscus season, memories come flooding back for Liebling Elizabeth Marlow — the young woman who, 70 years ago, made history as the inaugural winner of the Hibiscus Festival.

As Fiji experiences another Hibiscus celebration this year, Liebling remains the only woman to hold the distinction of being the country’s first Hibiscus queen.

But when the 18-year-old from Draunibota, Lami, entered the competition in 1956, there was little indication that she was about to become part of Fiji’s history.

“I was a young girl from Draunibota, Lami, away from the glare of the city,” she recalled.

“So taking part in the competition was new and challenging.”

The inaugural festival was a far cry from the colourful spectacle Fijians know today.

There were no elaborate floats, grand opening ceremonies or glittering crowns. The competition was held over two nights at the old Suva Town Hall, with more than 20 contestants taking part.

“Our engagement was only for two evenings,” Liebling said.

“We were put into a truck and rushed to the Old Town Hall, which was hot and uncomfortable.”

Her mother, Faga Bentley, was behing her wardrobe.

“For the first night, I wanted a red bag but it was brown, so my father took it to the PWD depot to have it spray-painted red so it could match my shoes,” she recalled with a laugh.

The competition itself was basic by today’s standards, but for Liebling it was an unforgettable experience.

The contestants were transported to the crowded Suva Town Hall, where they waited nervously behind heavy curtains before appearing before the judges.

On the final night the heat inside the hall was intense. Liebling also had another concern — her dress.

A problem with the dress had been cleverly secured by her mother, but Liebling remained worried that it might come undone while she was on stage.

Then came the moment that would change her life.

When her name was announced as the winner, the young Liebling was overwhelmed.

Rather than confidently stepping forward to accept her title, she burst into tears.

“I just stood there and cried and cried. My father was so happy.”

There was no crown for the queen’s brow,

“I did not wear a crown, just a sash to say I was Miss Hibiscus,” she recalled.

Her prize included a return trip to Australia, which she took in 1957. But the excitement of her new title was soon overshadowed by tragedy when her father became ill and later passed away.

Liebling found herself helping to support her family, carrying responsibilities far beyond those normally associated with a young beauty queen.

Yet through the decades, the memories of that first Hibiscus Festival have remained close to her heart.

From the humble beginnings at the old Suva Town Hall to the grand celebration the festival has become today, Liebling has watched generations of queens carry the Hibiscus title and represent Fiji.

To this year’s contestants, she has a simple message.

And if one of them is fortunate enough to wear the crown, Liebling has another reminder:

“Remember, if you win the crown, you will have to take Fiji and its people with you everywhere you go. Do this with pride.”

Seventy years after a young girl from Draunibota was unexpectedly crowned Fiji’s first Hibiscus queen, Liebling Marlow’s legacy remains woven into the story of the festival.

Her crown may never have existed, but her place in Hibiscus history is forever.

item.title: PEOPLE | A step towards independence
item.description: MAKING soap and tie-dye once seemed difficult to Seruwaia Cavabula, but after completing a training program in Sigatoka, she discovered that the skills could be learned and be turned into a source of income. Seruwaia is from Nausori Highlands in the district of Namataku in Navosa.
item.content:encoded:
MAKING soap and tie-dye once seemed difficult to Seruwaia Cavabula, but after completing a training program in Sigatoka, she discovered that the skills could be learned and be turned into a source of income.

Seruwaia is from Nausori Highlands in the district of Namataku in Navosa.

She lives in the village, where she helps look after her cousin and supports her family with work on their farm.

When she heard that training was being offered to village youths, she saw an opportunity to broaden her understanding and asked her parents for permission to attend.

“I thought it was hard to make soap or to print in tie-dye, but after undergoing the training I realised that it is quite easy to make, especially at home,” Seruwaia said.

The training, held at the Nasau Training Centre in Sigatoka, introduced her to skills she had previously only known as finished products.

“I’ve always heard about tie-dye, and I have even bought tie-dye products, but I never knew how to make it.”

Now, she wants to turn what she has learned into something of her own.

Seruwaia is the eldest of five siblings and the only girl in her family.

With her father working, she and the rest of the family help look after their farm. Their home is also some distance from the village, requiring a 10 to 15-minute walk to reach it.

Learning new skills is more than gaining knowledge for Seruwaia; it is a step towards creating an income and building a future for herself from home.

“The training that I’ve undertaken will surely guide me to earning an income as I will be able to produce items that I can sell in the village.”

“I will first go and try it out at home so I can perfect it and then continue to learn other skills as I go, so I can make products of my own in the future.”

Completing the training is only the beginning for Seruwaia.

She has plans she hopes to achieve, and she sees the skills she has gained as her first step.

For a young woman living in the village, that first step could open the way to new skills, new opportunities and eventually an income she can create for herself.

item.title: PEOPLE | Rooted in the dream
item.description: FOR 20-year-old Kubualagi Loa, the dream of playing professional rugby is growing alongside more than 1000 yaqona plants on his farm in Namoli Village, in the district of Noikoro, Navosa. Loa, the third eldest of six siblings, lives with his parents and balances farming with his passion for rugby.
item.content:encoded:
FOR 20-year-old Kubualagi Loa, the dream of playing professional rugby is growing alongside more than 1000 yaqona plants on his farm in Namoli Village, in the district of Noikoro, Navosa.

Loa, the third eldest of six siblings, lives with his parents and balances farming with his passion for rugby.

When he is not on the field, he is working on the farm, where he is building a future that he hopes will help take him closer to his sporting ambitions.

His rugby journey took shape while he attended Nasinu Secondary School from 2021 to 2025.

There, he played in the Deans Competition in 2025.

He now takes part in district competitions whenever he can.

But for Loa rugby is more than a game, it is a dream he hopes to turn into a career.

It is also his way of helping support his parents and contribute to the needs of his family.

He hopes the income from farming will give him greater financial stability while allowing him to continue pursuing opportunities in rugby.

He was supposed to be part of the Navosa team, but financial constraints prevented him from making the opportunity a reality.

Instead of giving up, Loa has turned to the land.

“I have planted over 1000 yaqona plants back in the farm,” he said.

The path has not been easy, but his ambition remains the same.

He hopes to continue playing rugby and one day represent Navosa or even Fiji.

For now, Loa is keeping his options open.

He is hopeful that other employment or rugby opportunities will come his way, while continuing to work the land and develop his yaqona farm.

item.title: PEOPLE | Selling with dignity
item.description: Turning roadside trade into family strengthBy the roadside in Vatukarasa Village, Nadroga, two women sit beside their laid out sulu laden with fresh produce. For them, the bustling roadside, full of passing vehicles and pedestrians, is more than a place to sell. It is a way of keep their families going.
item.content:encoded:
Turning roadside trade into family strengthBy the roadside in Vatukarasa Village, Nadroga, two women sit beside their laid out sulu laden with fresh produce.

For them, the bustling roadside, full of passing vehicles and pedestrians, is more than a place to sell. It is a way of keep their families going.

Adi Kelera Vakatovo, from Nukuilau, Navosa, is a mother of three, with two children in primary school. Together with her friend Inise Sauvana of Wainiyavu, Namosi, she has been selling food along the roadside for the past month.

Before this, the women sold their produce at the Sigatoka Municipal Market on weekends.

Today, they sell from Monday to Friday at Vatukarasa, earning enough to help meet household expenses and pay bills.

“With the price of groceries going up, we decided to help our husbands financially support the family,” they said.

Much of what they sell comes from their individual backyard gardens, while other items are sourced through market middlemen.

For Adi Kelera, the work is not about making a fortune but doing her part to keep everyone alive.

She believes women play an important role in the home by cleaning, cooking, caring for children and looking after the health of their families.

But she also believes women can contribute beyond the household when circumstances demand it.

Adi Kelera did not pursue a professional career after high school. Later in life, she realised she could stand beside her husband and help shoulder the responsibilities of raising a family.

Selling by the roadside, sometimes under the hot sun or in the rain, may not always feel glamorous. But Adi Kelera refuses to see it as shameful.

Her message to other women is: never look down on yourself.

“For women out there, every sale counts. Every dollar earned helps put food on the table, pay a bill and keep their families moving forward,” she said.

“There is dignity in honest work—and strength in a woman willing to do whatever she can for the people she loves .”

“There’s no shame in that but something we should be proud of\.”

Adi Kelera (right) and her friend, Inise Sauvana (left) sell their produce on the roadside at Vatukarasa Village in Nadroga. Picture: JOHN KAMEA

item.title: PEOPLE I Learning beyond the village
item.description: AT 24, Raijeli Naceva is learning that motherhood does not have to mean putting her own dreams on hold. For the young mother from Nausori Highland in Namataku, Navosa, every short course is another opportunity to learn something new and build a future in the village.
item.content:encoded:
AT 24, Raijeli Naceva is learning that motherhood does not have to mean putting her own dreams on hold.

For the young mother from Nausori Highland in Namataku, Navosa, every short course is another opportunity to learn something new and build a future in the village.

Raijeli, who has maternal links to the area, grew up in a farming family.

Her parents are farmers, and she is the eldest of six children, with her younger siblings still attending school.

Today, she and her husband, who is also from Nausori Highland, are raising their two-year-old daughter while running a small yaqona farm.

“You know life in the village – it’s mainly chores for us women,” Raijeli said.

For her family, yaqona farming is an important source of livelihood, but Raijeli is also looking beyond the farm, using short courses to broaden her skills and understanding.

She attended Ratu Nalewavada Public School in Nausori Highlands before continuing at Nadi Sangam College from Form 3 to Form 6.

She completed Form 7 at Ratu Navula College before pursuing a Certificate III in Age Care and Community Care.

The course changed how she viewed caring for elderly family members.

“What I learned in age care has broadened my understanding of how to take care of elderly in the family,” she said.

One lesson that stayed with her was the importance of food.

Raijeli learned that what elderly people eat can have a significant impact on their health, particularly when they continue eating foods they have been advised to avoid by the hospital.

She responded by reducing those foods and introducing healthier alternatives available in the village.

Now, her latest learning experience has opened another possibility.

Raijeli took part in tie-dye training, an experience she enjoyed.

“I liked that I was part of it,” she said.

Her goal is to start a small tie-dye business in the village, where she sees a demand for the products.

For Raijeli, learning is becoming part of everyday life alongside motherhood, farming and village responsibilities.

The tie-dye training was part of the buildup to the Navosa Youth Festival held last week.

item.title: PEOPLE | Turning farm labour into opportunity
item.description: WHEN the crowds began arriving at Vatureba Park for the Navosa Youth Festival, Kinisalote Rakai was already at work. At the entrance to the park, the 43-year-old farmer from Nukuilau Village in Draubuta, Navosa, had set up her makeshift stall with freshly harvested watermelons.
item.content:encoded:
WHEN the crowds began arriving at Vatureba Park for the Navosa Youth Festival, Kinisalote Rakai was already at work.

At the entrance to the park, the 43-year-old farmer from Nukuilau Village in Draubuta, Navosa, had set up her makeshift stall with freshly harvested watermelons.

Some were cut into juicy portions for festival-goers looking for something cool in the hot weather, while whole melons were ready for those wanting to take one home.

The location proved to be a good choice.

As people entered the festival, many stopped at Rakai’s stall to buy the affordable watermelon.

By midday, almost 80 of the more than 100 watermelons, she had brought with her husband, had been sold.

“We have been farming for a while, and watermelon has been one of our longest crops as it grows well in the province,” Rakai said.

For Rakai, selling the family’s produce is another part of the work she shares with her husband.

Their farm has been producing watermelons since 1999.

Over 27 years, they have also grown cabbages, tomatoes, capsicum, long beans, bora beans, French beans, corn, peanuts, watermelons and sweet potatoes.

The couple leases land and uses a tractor to help with the work.

They once had a carrier but sold it to buy the tractor because it would help them more in running the farm.

Getting their produce to the market, however, comes at a cost.

Transporting the watermelons from Nukuilau Village to Vatureba Park costs them $180.

The Rakai couple has seven children. After the death of their eldest child, they now care for their six children with what they earn from farming.

She said their experience had shown them that the weather in Navosa allowed certain vegetables to grow well, giving the family an opportunity to earn from the land.

For Rakai, farming is a partnership, and she wants other women to see the value of being part of that partnership.

“I would like to encourage women, who are at home, to always assist your husband if he farms,” she said.

“We can earn a lot if we help each other out in toiling the land.”

At the festival, each watermelon sold was a small return on years of shared labour.

item.title: PEOPLE | From training to trade | New skill builds business hope
item.description: A TWO-DAY training at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga has changed how Joave Doidoi views earning an income. The young man from Draiba Village in the Namataku district of Navosa plans to turn his newly acquired tie-dye skills into a business at home.
item.content:encoded:
A TWO-DAY training at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga has changed how Joave Doidoi views earning an income.

The young man from Draiba Village in the Namataku district of Navosa plans to turn his newly acquired tie-dye skills into a business at home.

With a bubbly personality and an easy manner, Joave spoke enthusiastically about what he learned during the short course.

He was among participants who later showcased their creations at the recent Navosa Youth Festival, an experience that opened his eyes to the possibilities of his new skills.

“Attending the tie-dye and soap making training session lifted many of the worries I had about earning an income,” Joave said.

“I realised from the training session that it’s easy to earn an income right in the village.”

The training also broadened his understanding of how everyday materials could be transformed into income-generating products.

“This has deepened our knowledge, especially on how to use everyday materials at home to make income-generating products like soap, for instance,” he said.

Joave had previously completed a Level 3 Certificate in Catering and Commercial Cookery. When he heard about the tie-dye course, he seized the opportunity.

“When I heard about the tie-dye course, I quickly jumped at the opportunity because I would acquire new skills from it in just two days,” he said.

Although originally from Draiba Village, Joave currently lives at Natao Settlement. He intends to take his skills back home and put them into practice.

“I can see myself starting my own business in the village,” he said.

“I’m planning to go home and actually make something out of what I’ve learned instead of leaving it aside again.”

For Joave, the next step is turning training into action.

He hopes young people who gain skills can receive further support, particularly financial assistance to help establish their projects.

“I can start my own tie-dye project or help others learn about it,” he said.

The two-day training has given him more than a skill — it has given him a plan: to take knowledge home, create products and build an income from his village doorstep.

item.title: PEOPLE I Skill to wealth
item.description: AT 19, Ivamere Finau Kaitoga has already learned that setbacks do not have to determine the direction of a young person’s life. Growing up in Nausori Highlands, in the district of Namataku, Nadroga/Navosa, Ivamere was raised by her mother after her father died when she was only 11 months old.
item.content:encoded:
AT 19, Ivamere Finau Kaitoga has already learned that setbacks do not have to determine the direction of a young person’s life.

Growing up in Nausori Highlands, in the district of Namataku, Nadroga/Navosa, Ivamere was raised by her mother after her father died when she was only 11 months old.

Her mother became the family’s main support and from a young age, Ivamere learnt to stand beside her.

School was one of the challenges she faced.

After completing Form 5, Ivamere left high school and began searching for a different path to shape her future.

She went on to study Business Administration at Pacific Polytech, a decision that would become an important stepping stone in her journey.

During this time, she lived with her uncle in Ba, however, when her uncle’s home was destroyed by a fire, Ivamere was forced to return to her village.

Back home she joined other young people in yaqona farming, a common livelihood for youths in Nausori Highlands.

Her family also depend on her mother, who operates a small canteen from home, grows vegetables and sells produce at the Nadi market, to help meet the family’s daily expenses.

Ivamere and her siblings help their mother every day.

Then came an opportunity that gave the young woman a new way of looking at what was possible.

Ivamere took part in tie-dye training organised by the Ministry of Youth and Sports at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga.

For her, the training was more than learning how to create colourful designs. It opened her eyes to the possibility of turning a skill into an income-generating activity while remaining in the village.

“The training has broadened my knowledge and has allowed me to learn a new skill,” she said.

“It was an eye-opener for me as a young woman living in the village, it has taught me that we can earn an income from these types of skills even while living in the village.”

The experience has given Ivamere something to take home besides the skill itself: A plan.

She wants to continue practising tie-dye, create materials in the village and share what she has learnt with her family.

Her aim is to improve her skills until the craft can become a source of income.

Her experience in business administration may also prove useful as she works towards that goal.

Ivamere hopes to combine what she learnt in her studies with her new tie-dye skills.

For a young woman, who faced the loss of her father as an infant, struggled at school and returned to the village after her family lost their home, the future now looks different.

Ivamere is not simply returning home with a new skill, she is returning with an idea of what that skill could become in the future.
